prompt: Which of these is the interest on Coreto's seat-hold debt, in the lesson's sense?
hint: One of them is paid once; the interest is paid again each sprint.

choices.text: The 320 hours it would take to remove the row locks for good
choices.why: That is the principal: the one-off cost of paying the debt off, which nobody is forced to spend.

choices.text: The sales lost when a big on-sale fails
choices.why: Lost sales are a risk, priced in lesson 20 as a probability times a loss; the interest counts hours.

choices.text: The 31 extra hours paid each sprint while the locks stay
choices.why: Right: interest is the extra time paid on each change while the debt stays, with nobody deciding to pay it.

choices.text: R$ 48,000, the fix priced at R$ 150 an hour
choices.why: That is still the principal, only written in reais instead of hours.

prompt: Match each description to what it is in the lesson's vocabulary.
hint: Ask who pays it, and when.

pairs.left: Paid once, and only if somebody decides to
Paid each sprint by whoever works near the code
Sales lost when an on-sale fails
pairs.right: A risk, priced as probability times loss

pairs.left: A tangled module nobody has edited for years
pairs.right: A mess that charges nothing this sprint

prompt: The old reporting replica has the second-largest principal of Coreto's four debts. Why does the lesson rank it last?
hint: Look at the other column.

choices.text: Its interest is 4 hours a sprint, the lowest
choices.why: Right: a big principal with little interest is a bill nobody has to pay, and it costs almost nothing while it waits.

choices.text: Reports matter less to venues than checkout does
choices.why: That may be true, and it is not the lesson's reason; the ranking comes from the hours it charges.

choices.text: Its principal estimate is the least reliable of the four
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson questions that estimate; even a perfect one would leave the replica last.

choices.text: The Data team has already planned to rebuild it next year
choices.why: No such plan exists in the lesson, and a plan would not change what the debt costs each sprint.

prompt: A team wants 400 hours to untangle a billing module that nobody has changed in three years and that has caused no incident. By the lesson's reasoning, what is the case for doing it now?
hint: Interest is paid on change.

choices.text: Strong, since 400 hours makes it the largest debt in the register
choices.why: That reads the principal as the size of the problem, which is the mistake the lesson opens with.

choices.text: Weak: code nobody changes charges no interest yet
choices.why: Right: with no changes and no incidents there is no interest, and the 400 hours would return nothing until somebody starts working there.

choices.text: Strong, because old code gets worse each year it is left
choices.why: Code that nobody touches does not change by itself; debt grows when code is built on top of it.

choices.text: Weak, because billing belongs to the Payments team's own roadmap
choices.why: Who owns the module does not decide whether the debt costs anything; the hours paid on it do.

prompt: Davi is adding up the seat-hold debt's interest. Which of these belong in it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only the extra hours count, and each failure is counted once.

choices.text: Reviewers' hours on changes that touch the module
choices.why: Yes: at Coreto most of the tax on changes lands on the reviewers, and leaving them out undercounts it.

choices.text: Hours worked on incidents whose cause names the module
choices.why: Yes: incident hours are one of the three sources, and the incident log already records them.

choices.text: Sales lost during a failed on-sale
choices.why: Those are the risk lesson 20 prices; putting them here as well would count one failure twice.

choices.text: A team's time building a feature it would have built anyway
choices.why: The feature's own hours are not interest; only the extra hours the debt adds to it are.

prompt: Why does the lesson reject a meeting where engineers say how much each debt costs them?
hint: Measured on the work, not on the mood.

choices.text: Engineers overstate debt to get time for refactoring
choices.why: The lesson accuses nobody of bad faith; the problem is that a feeling is not a count of hours.

choices.text: A meeting costs more engineer-hours than the debt
choices.why: A meeting is cheap next to 55 hours a sprint of interest; its cost is not the objection.

choices.text: Managers, not engineers, own the budget that pays for the debt
choices.why: Who holds the budget does not change how the hours are counted, and the engineers' own tags are one of the sources.

choices.text: The loudest complaint wins, and annoyance is not cost
choices.why: Right: the debt that annoys most is rarely the one that costs most, so the answers measure the mood.

prompt: Suppose the seat-hold interest is really half of Davi's 31 hours a sprint. With the principal still at 320 hours, what is the payback in sprints? Round to one decimal place.
hint: Principal divided by interest; half of 31 is 15.5.

prompt: Another company measures the tax on a module by comparing only how long the authors of changes took. Reviews of those changes need three teams. What happens to the measured interest?
hint: Where did most of Coreto's seat-hold tax land?

choices.text: It comes out too high, because the authors count their waiting time
choices.why: Waiting is part of the tax; the bigger problem is the reviewers' hours, which this method leaves out.

choices.text: It comes out too low, missing the hours that land on the reviewers
choices.why: Right: when reviews need three teams, much of the tax is the reviewers' time, and counting authors alone undercounts it.

choices.text: It is right, since review time is part of normal work
choices.why: Ordinary review is normal; three teams reviewing because of the debt is extra, and the extra is the interest.

choices.text: It is unaffected, as only incident hours really measure interest
choices.why: Incident hours are one of three sources; the tax on changes is the largest part of most interest.

prompt: A fifth debt turns up: a principal of 90 hours and an interest of 15 hours a sprint. What is its payback, in sprints?
hint: Principal divided by interest.

prompt: In the sheet, column D divides each debt's principal by its ___ to give the payback in sprints.
hint: Column C: hours a sprint.

prompt: In the payback sheet, what does =SUM(E2:E5) return, and what does that number mean?
hint: Column E is interest a year, in reais.

choices.text: 720, the hours to pay off the four debts
choices.why: 720 hours is the sum of the principals in column B, not of column E.

choices.text: 8250, what the four debts cost each sprint
choices.why: That is =SUM(C2:C5)*150, the cost of one sprint; column E is a whole year.

choices.text: 86.3, the sprints it would take to pay the four back
choices.why: Adding paybacks gives nothing meaningful, and column E does not hold paybacks.

choices.text: 214500, the reais of interest the four charge in a year
choices.why: Right: R$ 214,500 a year, spent without appearing on any budget line, for debts nobody decided to pay.

prompt: The payback ranks the flaky suite first, at 5.7 sprints, while Coreto's strategy puts the seat-hold debt first. How does the lesson reconcile the two?
hint: What does the payback count, and what does it leave out?

choices.text: The strategy is wrong and should be changed to follow the sheet
choices.why: The sheet informs the strategy and does not overrule it; it counts hours and not the risk of a failed on-sale.

choices.text: Hours miss the on-sale risk, and the suite is cheap to fix as well
choices.why: Right: the seat-hold debt carries the risk the diagnosis named, and an 80-hour fix with a quick payback does not compete with it.

choices.text: The payback should be computed in reais instead of hours
choices.why: Both sides are priced at the same R$ 150 an hour, so the ranking would not move at all.

choices.text: The seat-hold payback of 10.3 sprints is too short to trust
choices.why: The lesson shows that even half the interest leaves the seat-hold debt ahead of the replica; precision is not the issue.

prompt: Why does the seat-hold debt's interest rise by about 2 hours a sprint?
hint: What keeps being written around the row locks?

choices.text: The engineers who knew the code are leaving
choices.why: Nobody leaves in the lesson; the rise comes from new code built on the debt.

choices.text: Ticket volume grows each month, loading the database harder
choices.why: Load explains failures in on-sales, a risk; the interest is hours spent on changes, and those rise with the workarounds.

choices.text: New features keep being written around the locks
choices.why: Right: every workaround is one more thing to rehearse, review and keep working, so the interest after it is higher.

choices.text: The hourly rate of R$ 150 goes up each sprint
choices.why: The rate is fixed in the course; the growth is in hours, before any rate is applied.

prompt: The seat-hold interest is 31 hours in sprint 1 and rises by 2 hours each sprint. How many hours of interest are paid in sprint 6 alone?
hint: Sprint 6 is five rises after sprint 1.

prompt: Besides paying the principal, what does the lesson say fights a growing debt, and which of Coreto's actions does it?
hint: The interest rises because code keeps being built on the debt.

choices.text: Stopping growth: Reservations reviews each change
choices.why: Right: review by an owner cuts the number of new workarounds, which is what makes the interest rise.

choices.text: Measuring it: the load test that replays an on-sale
choices.why: The load test measures the fix against an on-sale; it does not stop features being built around the locks.

choices.text: Raising the rate: pricing each hour of the seat-hold work above R$ 150
choices.why: A higher rate changes how big the number looks, not how fast the hours grow.

choices.text: Waiting: the freeze before big on-sales
choices.why: The freeze protects the on-sale while the work is under way; it does not reduce the workarounds written the rest of the year.

prompt: Two debts each show a payback of 12 sprints today. One sits in code three teams build on each sprint; the other in a module nobody adds to. Which goes first, by the lesson?
hint: Whose payback will still be 12 next quarter?

choices.text: Either, since equal paybacks make them equal investments
choices.why: The paybacks are equal today; one of them is getting worse while you wait and the other is not.

choices.text: The quiet module, so the busy code settles down first
choices.why: The busy code will not settle by itself: each sprint of building on it adds interest and, often, principal.

choices.text: The one teams build on, since its interest is rising
choices.why: Right: a flat debt can wait on its payback, and a growing one gets more expensive to leave each sprint.

choices.text: Neither, until both have been measured for a year
choices.why: Measuring twice, a quarter apart, is enough to see a trend; a year of waiting is a year of rising interest.

prompt: Put Coreto's four debts in order of payback, shortest first.
hint: Principal divided by interest, for each one.
trap: Ordering by principal puts the seat-hold locking last and the replica third; the payback moves the seat-hold debt to second and the replica to the bottom.

prompt: Davi has one sentence to put the seat-hold debt to Otávio, the CFO. Which one answers the question a budget asks?
hint: What happens if the money is not spent?

choices.text: We need 320 hours of refactoring in the reservation module
choices.why: That is the principal as a request, and to a CFO it reads as engineers wanting to tidy up.

choices.text: The reservation code is the worst in coreto-core
choices.why: An opinion about quality says nothing about cost; a mess nobody touches would fit the same sentence.

choices.text: It costs R$ 120,900 a year until we spend R$ 48,000 once
choices.why: Right: a recurring cost against a one-off investment is the shape a CFO decides in, and it says what not spending costs.

choices.text: Fixing the locks raises availability towards 99.99% on on-sale days
choices.why: That is how the strategy measures success; it does not put a price on leaving the debt.

prompt: A payback in the sheet rests on assumptions. Which of these does the lesson say to check before quoting one? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are named at the end of the sheet section.

choices.text: That paying the principal removes the interest entirely
choices.why: Yes: a half-finished fix removes part of the interest, and the sheet then overstates the return.

choices.text: That the interest stays where it is while you wait
choices.why: Yes: for a growing debt the flat payback is the optimistic case.

choices.text: That the R$ 150 rate matches each engineer's salary
choices.why: The rate is a loaded average, and the payback in sprints does not use it at all: hours divide by hours.

choices.text: That the principal includes the lost sales of a failed on-sale
choices.why: Lost sales belong to neither column; they are the risk lesson 20 adds beside them.

prompt: A debt charges 10 hours of interest a sprint. With 26 sprints a year and an engineer-hour at R$ 150, what does it cost in a year, in reais?
hint: The same product as column E: hours × 26 × 150.
